blocks.text: Dear Ms. Frazier:

This letter sets out the terms on which our firm will advise {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} on the rationalization of its operating footprint, and it becomes our agreement at the moment you countersign the copy enclosed with it and return that copy to me. I have written it at some length, and in plainer language than such letters usually carry, because an engagement of this kind proceeds more surely when both sides have read the same account of it before any work is begun. I would ask you, before you sign, to read what follows against your own sense of the assignment we discussed, and to tell me of any point on which the two do not yet sit comfortably together.
The Work and How We Propose to Approach It

The assignment is a rationalization of the footprint through which {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} carries on its operations, by which I mean the network of sites the company runs and the question of whether that network, taken as a whole, still fits the demand it was built to serve. We will begin by assembling a faithful picture of the footprint as it stands today, recording what each location costs to hold and to operate, how fully it is used, and what part it plays in serving the business, so that no site is judged on impression where a measured figure can be had instead. From that baseline we will develop and weigh options for a smaller or differently arranged network, setting against each of them the cost it would release, the service it would place at risk, and the disruption it would ask the organization to absorb, and we will describe those trade-offs plainly, including the ones that a preferred option would require you to accept.

It is worth being as clear about the limits of the work as about its substance. This is a study of the footprint and a set of recommendations you will be equipped to act on; it is not the execution of any closure, consolidation, or move, and the carrying out of whatever you decide will remain yours to lead unless we later agree, in writing, on a separate engagement to support it. Should the shape of the assignment change materially once we are under way, whether at your request or because the analysis brings something unexpected to light, I will describe the change and settle its terms with you before we act on it, so that nothing is ever added to the work without your assent having been given first.
Who Will Carry the Work

The work will be done by a small and consistent team. Cynthia Hart, a research associate of the firm, will ground the study in the market and operating context that surrounds the footprint, and will assemble the situation assessment on which the later analysis rests. Deborah Gordon, a senior associate, will own the benchmarking and the site-level cost and utilization data, and will be answerable for ensuring that the figures we present can be defended against a hard question rather than merely asserted. Brenda Clayton, a consultant, will do the analytical work behind the exhibits, from the reconciliation of the underlying data through to the option comparisons themselves. I will keep my own hand on the engagement at the points where a judgment must be made about how far a finding can be pressed before it outruns what the evidence will bear, and nothing of consequence will leave the firm under our name without my having read it first.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is fixed at {{fact:f:E-2017-001.fee}}, which covers the time of the people named above through the expected close of the work, together with the ordinary meetings, correspondence, and interim materials that accompany an assignment of this kind. It does not extend to work we might later agree to add, such as support for the execution of your decisions, which we would scope and price separately before beginning it, nor to the incidental costs of the work, such as travel or the reproduction of materials, which we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us. We will render invoices against the fixed fee at regular intervals as the work proceeds, and each invoice will fall due within thirty days of its date.
Term and Termination

The engagement will commence on {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}} and is scoped to run for something on the order of seven months, that being the period over which we have planned the assessment, the analysis, and the design of the options, though I will tell you early if the work proves to need more time or less. Either of us may bring the engagement to an end on fourteen days' written notice to the other. Should you choose to end it, you will owe our fee earned to the date of termination together with any costs properly committed to that point, and nothing beyond that; should we do so, which we would undertake only for a reason our professional standards required of us, we will return any part of the fee that relates to work not yet performed and will assist an orderly handover of the assignment.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use solely for the purpose of the engagement you have retained us to perform. That obligation binds every member of the team, it survives the completion or termination of the work, and it extends to the fact of our involvement as fully as it does to its substance. We would ask the same of you in respect of the methods, analyses, and written materials we bring to the assignment, which represent the firm's own way of working, and neither of us will disclose the other's confidential information except where the law or a proper authority compels it, and then only so far as we are compelled and, where it is practicable to do so, on notice to the other.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform this engagement with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm retained for it, and our advice will represent our considered professional judgment on the information available to us. We do not, however, warrant any particular commercial result, since what an operating footprint finally yields depends in large part on decisions and actions that will rest with your organization rather than with ours, and on conditions in the markets you serve that neither of us controls. Save to the extent that the law does not permit such a limit, our aggregate liability to you arising out of or in connection with this engagement will be limited to the fees actually paid to us under it, and neither of us will be liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss.
Governing Law

This letter, together with the signature page that accompanies it, constitutes the entire agreement between us in respect of this engagement and supersedes any prior discussion or understanding, and it may be varied only by a writing signed by both of us. It will be governed by, and construed in accordance with, the law of the state in which our firm maintains its principal office, and each of us submits to the jurisdiction of the courts of that state in respect of any dispute arising under it; should any single provision of this letter be held unenforceable, the remainder of it will continue in force, unaffected.

If this letter reflects the understanding we reached, I would be grateful if you would sign and date the enclosed copy where indicated and return it to me, keeping the other for your file; once your signed copy is in our hands, Cynthia Hart will write to you to arrange the first meetings and the opening requests for information, so that we can begin without delay. If any part of it warrants discussion first, tell me and I will make the time this week to talk it through before you sign.
Sincerely,

To: Deborah Gordon; Brenda Clayton
From: Cynthia Hart, Research Associate
Re: Footprint Rationalization for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} -- kickoff and plan of work

The engagement opened on {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}}. Our charge is to rationalize the operating footprint of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}. That comes down to one question above the rest: does the current network of sites still fit the demand the business has to serve. Sandra Frazier, their VP Finance, is our sponsor. She has asked for choices her own managers can act on, not a study that reads well and then sits on a shelf.

The standard she set should govern how we work. We build to a figure that can be traced, and we mark plainly where the evidence thins out. If we hold to that, the recommendation will survive the first hard look. That is the whole aim of the early weeks, and it is worth saying out loud before the pressure to reach an answer builds.
The shape of the work

The work falls into four parts, run in sequence rather than at once. The first is the baseline. We map every site in the footprint, what it costs to hold and to run, and how much of it the business actually uses. A site is judged on that record, not on reputation, and not on how it was described to us.

The second is the cost and utilization picture behind the map. Deborah Gordon owns it. She will set the first site-level data requests to Sandra Frazier's team in the opening week, kept short so we are not held up. What comes back she will benchmark against a comparator set we agree with the client, so that high cost at a site is measured against a like standard rather than an impression of what a site of that kind should cost.

The third is the option work. Brenda Clayton will build the comparisons that test two or three shapes for the network against the baseline. Each option is priced for the cost it releases and the service it puts at risk, and the two are shown together, never one without the other. We do not show an option before the baseline is solid, because an option built on a soft baseline comes apart the first time it meets a fact from the floor.

The fourth is the transition. Once a direction is chosen, we lay out the order in which the client can carry it through without us in the room. That part waits on the rest. It is named here only so the end is in view from the start, since a recommendation the client cannot sequence is not much use to them.
The first two weeks

A few things need to close early. Deborah Gordon's first data request should reach Sandra Frazier by the end of week one, kept deliberately narrow so we are not waiting on a long list before we can begin. Brenda Clayton and I will agree the comparator set before it goes out, so the data arrives in a form we can use rather than one we have to rework.

There is also the market context to stand up. I will pull the demand picture for the regions the sites serve, so that when a location looks weak on cost we already know whether the demand behind it is growing or thinning. That read shapes which sites are candidates to consolidate and which are better left alone.

I will circulate a one-page schedule this week, with the client sessions and our own checkpoints marked on it. Please keep the first fortnight light on other commitments so we can set the pace early. If you can see a conflict coming, tell me now, while the dates are still ours to set.
Hello Sandra,

Thank you for the site list and the lease summary. They arrived in good order, and Deborah Gordon already has the cost and utilization work under way against them. The early read on the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} footprint is that it is more uneven than the summary alone suggests, with a handful of locations carrying cost out of proportion to how much they are actually used.

Two things would help us keep the baseline moving. Brenda Clayton needs read access to the last two years of occupancy and throughput figures behind the sites your team flagged. We would also like thirty minutes each with the two facility managers who know those locations best. If either request needs a sign-off on your side, tell me who to approach and I will take it up directly rather than leave it on your desk. For the two conversations, any half hour in the next two weeks works for us, so send whatever suits their calendars and we will fit around them.

I know this lands in a week that is likely already full, Sandra Frazier, and I have kept the asks as small as the work allows. Anything that is easiest to send can come straight to me, Cynthia Hart, and I will get it to the team the same day. I will keep this thread as the running record so nothing has to be chased twice.
Best
Working Session -- Footprint Rationalization for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}

The session settled one thing that sets up the rest: we will carry three candidate networks into the option review, not two, because the middle case splits the difference in a way the client wants tested on its own. The site baseline is closed. The cost and utilization picture is built and reconciled to it. What follows records who was present, what we covered, and who owns each next step.
Present
Where the baseline landed

Deborah Gordon walked the closed baseline. Every site is now tied to what it costs, how fully it is used, and the part it plays in serving demand. Two locations stand out. Both sit near the top of the network on cost and run well below half their capacity. Nothing in the data argues for keeping either of them as it is.

The reconciliation took longer than the map, which was expected. Two sites reported occupancy and throughput on different bases, so the raw figures were not comparable until Brenda Clayton restated them onto one. That is done, and the baseline now holds together well enough to build options on.
The options on the table

Brenda Clayton set out the three candidate networks. The first consolidates the two weak sites into the nearest hub. The second goes further and relocates a third. The third holds more capacity in reserve, against demand that Cynthia Hart's market read says is not yet settled. Each network is priced for the cost it releases and the service it puts at risk, so the review can weigh them on the same terms.

The middle case is the one the client asked us to keep. It saves less than the fuller consolidation but disturbs fewer served regions, and Sandra Frazier wanted that trade set out on its own rather than folded into the two extremes. Carrying three networks costs us little now and saves a round of rework later if the review lands between the ends.
What the client pressed on

Sandra Frazier pushed hardest on service. She has seen footprint cuts that looked clean on a map and cost the business a customer the next quarter. We agreed to carry a service and coverage measure alongside cost for every option, so a saving that comes at the price of coverage is visible before anyone commits to it.

She also asked that the numbers be ones her own team can rerun after we leave. That is already the standard we work to, and we confirmed it. Deborah Gordon will hand over the baseline in the form the client's finance team keeps its own data, so nothing has to be translated to be checked.
Action items

rows: Add a service and coverage measure to each of the three candidate networks and reconcile it to the cost picture
Rebuild the option comparisons to show cost and service side by side for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}
Firm up the demand read behind the reserve case so the third option rests on evidence, not caution
Confirm the two facility managers for the option review and clear access to the throughput detail

blocks.text: The next fixed point is the option review. Once the service measure is in, we compare the three networks in one sitting and narrow to the one worth planning a transition around.
Status Report -- Footprint Rationalization for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}

This report covers the engagement's middle stretch and is prepared for the client's finance leadership by Cynthia Hart, on behalf of the team. The work is on plan. The baseline is closed, the cost and utilization picture behind it is built and reconciled, and the option work is under way. Nothing to date has moved the engagement off its schedule or its budget.
Where things stand

The engagement is at its midpoint. The picture of the current footprint of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} is complete, and the analysis has turned from describing the network to deciding what shape it should take. The work still ahead is the comparison of the options and the plan for carrying the chosen one through.

The pace is steady rather than fast, and deliberately so. A footprint decision is expensive to reverse, so the early weeks were spent making the baseline one that will hold up. That patience is now paying off, because the options rest on measured figures rather than on assumptions.
What we have done this period

Deborah Gordon has closed the site-level cost and utilization baseline. It now ties every location to what it costs and how fully it is used, reconciled so that neither side has cause to argue later about a number. Two sites already stand out as high in cost and low in use.

Brenda Clayton has built the first option comparisons on top of that baseline. She is testing three candidate networks rather than two, so that a middle case is weighed on its own terms instead of being assumed away. The early finding is a familiar one: a small number of sites carry cost well out of proportion to the demand they serve.

We also held a working session with your team this period. The main outcome was to carry a service and coverage measure alongside cost for every option. That way no saving is adopted without its effect on service being visible first. The change is already built into the comparisons.

The reconciliation behind that baseline was the slower part of the period. Two sites had reported occupancy and throughput on different bases, and until Brenda Clayton restated them onto one, the figures could not be compared. That work is finished, and it is the reason the option comparisons can now be trusted.
What comes next

Over the coming weeks we will finish the option comparisons and narrow the three candidate networks to the one worth planning around. The service measure will sit beside cost in that comparison, so the choice is made on both at once rather than on cost with service considered afterward.

We will bring the narrowed option back to your team in a working session before it is fixed, so the choice is made with you rather than presented to you. The middle case, which saves less but disturbs fewer regions, will be shown on its own terms so that it is a real alternative and not a straw one.

Once a direction is set, we will lay out the sequence in which your team can carry it through. The aim is that the recommendation arrives with a route to acting on it, rather than as a conclusion left on its own.
Budget

The engagement remains within its fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.fee}}. That figure covers the team's time through the expected close of the work, and nothing has arisen that would take the assignment beyond the scope the fee was set against. Should anything of that kind appear, we would raise it with you and settle it before acting, as our engagement letter provides.
What could still get in the way

Two risks are worth naming while they are still small. The first is the throughput detail behind a handful of sites, which is thinner than the rest and could soften the service comparison if it does not firm up. We have asked your team for the underlying figures and expect them shortly.

The second is the reserve case, the option that holds more capacity against future demand. It rests on a demand read that is not yet settled. We are firming up that read now, and we will not lean on the reserve case until the evidence behind it will bear the weight.

On balance the engagement is where it should be at the halfway mark, with the current footprint understood and the options taking shape. We will come back to you with the narrowed option and its trade-offs before any direction is fixed.
Working Session -- Footprint Rationalization for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}

The session closed on the recommendation: consolidate the two weakest sites into the regional hub, and hold the third under review for a year rather than move it now. The service measure held up under the client's questions. What remains is the transition plan and the final report. These minutes record who attended, what was decided, and who carries each remaining task.
Present
The recommendation

Deborah Gordon presented the final comparison. Consolidating the two high-cost, low-use sites into the regional hub releases the most cost while leaving service coverage intact on the measure we agreed. Relocating the third site saves less and puts a served region at risk, so we do not recommend it now. Holding it under review for a year keeps the option open without paying to exercise it.

The three networks were shown side by side, cost and service together. The recommended one is not the deepest cut; it is the one where the saving does not come at the expense of a region the business still serves. Deborah Gordon was clear that the fuller consolidation looks better on cost alone, and worse the moment service is put next to it.
Where the client pushed

Sandra Frazier tested the service case hard, as she has throughout. She wanted to know whether the hub can absorb the consolidated volume without a fall in service. The utilization figures say it can, with room to spare, and Brenda Clayton walked the numbers behind that.

Cynthia Hart added that the demand read for the third site is still soft, which is the reason it stays under review rather than moving. Sandra Frazier accepted that, on the condition that the review has a date and an owner rather than being left open indefinitely. We agreed to fix both in the transition plan.
Transition

We agreed the transition matters as much as the recommendation itself. {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} will carry out any consolidation with its own people, so the plan has to be one the client's team can run. Deborah Gordon will set out the sequence and the timing. Brenda Clayton will attach the cost and service effect to each step, so the client can see what each move buys and what it risks before committing to it.

The order of steps was discussed but not fixed. The sense in the room was to move the smaller of the two sites first, learn from it, and carry what is learned into the larger move rather than run both at once. Sandra Frazier preferred that to a single switch, on the ground that a staged move is easier to stop or slow if service shows any strain.
Action items

rows: Draft the transition sequence for the hub consolidation, with timing for each step
Attach the cost and service effect to each step of the transition and finalize the exhibits
Write the demand note that supports holding the third site under review for a year
Confirm the internal owners on the client side who will run the consolidation

blocks.text: The next step is the transition plan. With the recommendation settled, the remaining work is to make it something the client can act on, and to set that down in the final report.
